title: Logic: yes, no, and, or, not
summary: How a program decides: every test answers yes or no, and not, and, or combine those answers.

scheme: 0          ← yes: alice is on the list
text: Every command answers a question when it ends: did it work? That answer is its exit status.
- 0 means yes, it worked. Any other number means no (grep: 1 for not found, 2 for an error).
- $? holds the answer of the last command.
- -q tells grep to stay quiet: only the answer counts. -x matches whole lines only, so al doesn't find alice.
if runs a command and takes one road or the other depending on its answer.
- then: what to do when the answer is yes. else (optional): when it's no.
- fi closes the if: it's if written backwards.
That is how a program decides: it asks a yes/no question, then picks a road.
[ ] is a command made for questions: it answers yes or no, like grep -q.
- Keep a space after [ and before ]: [-f x] is not understood.
- Put variables in double quotes: an empty one would break the test.
$ if [ -d backup ]; then echo 'ready'; fi

scheme: = if the name is NOT on the list
text: ! turns an answer around: read it aloud as NOT.
- Leave a space after it: ! grep, not !grep. Inside a test too: [ ! -f notes.txt ].
- It's one character, easy to add or forget: a guard with one ! too many lets in exactly the people it should keep out.
Read your conditions aloud: the sentence must say what you mean.
&& (AND) says yes only when both answers are yes. || (OR) says yes as soon as one of them is yes.
- To copy a file into a folder, you need the file AND the folder: &&.
- Bash stops as soon as it knows: a && b runs b only if a said yes, a || b only if a said no.
$ mkdir backup || echo 'could not create it'
Every language has the same three words: not, and, or. Only the spelling changes.
- Watch the last column: for bash, 0 means yes (it worked). In Python and C, 0 means false.
- Before Python or C, make sure you can read a condition aloud and say when it's true.
